analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans buy identical prescription drugs from certified Canadian pharmacies at Canadian prices.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a Republican and a Democrat with 9 cosponsors, never received a committee hearing or a vote and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Health and Human Services to write rules, within 180 days, allowing individuals to import prescription drugs they bought themselves from approved Canadian pharmacies. Imports would be limited to a 90-day personal supply with a valid US prescription, and would have to be identical in ingredient, dose, and form to FDA-approved drugs. Drugs like controlled substances, biologics, and refrigerated medications would be excluded. The bill never moved past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay high out-of-pocket prescription costs — especially the uninsured and people with high deductibles — who could fill 90-day prescriptions from certified Canadian pharmacies, where identical drugs sell for far less than in the United States.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People paying US drug prices out of pocket

how_it_helps.text: Individuals could import up to a 90-day personal supply of a prescription drug from an approved Canadian pharmacy, filled with a valid US prescription, holding the same active ingredients, dosage form, and strength as the FDA-approved version.

HHS would have to certify Canadian pharmacies that meet standards for licensing, quality assurance, and compliance, and publish an FDA list of approved pharmacies so consumers know which sellers are vetted.
Controls substances, biologics, intravenous and infused drugs, refrigerated drugs, and other higher-risk categories would be excluded from importation.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would lose some US sales at US prices to imports priced at Canadian levels; taxpayers would fund the FDA's pharmacy certification and oversight work.

drawbacks.text: The exclusions cover many of the most expensive modern treatments, including biologics, monoclonal antibodies, and refrigerated drugs, so the savings would not reach patients on those medicines.

Personal importation of drugs is restricted in US law largely out of safety concern, because regulators cannot fully verify drugs bought abroad; this bill addresses that by limiting imports to certified, long-established Canadian pharmacies with testing requirements, but the safety oversight burden would rest on a certification system FDA would have to build and enforce.
The bill addresses only personal importation, capped at a 90-day supply, and leaves US drug prices themselves untouched, so it would not fix the underlying price gap.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people paying hundreds of dollars a month for brand-name drugs, a legal, vetted channel to Canadian prices is a real and immediate benefit, and the bill's certification and screening rules are a good-faith answer to the safety objection. Its main limitation is scope: the excluded categories include many of the costliest drugs, so it would help some patients more than others and would not lower US list prices directly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on January 8, 2015, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it; the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John McCain (R-AZ) introduced the bill on January 8, 2015, with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-MN) as co-lead.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was recorded for the rest of the 114th Congress, and the bill died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who kept the US market free of lower-priced Canadian imports for another two years; Americans buying drugs at US prices gained nothing.

for.role: US Senator from Arizona; bill sponsor

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred to the committee on January 8, 2015.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and their trade association (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Opposed drug importation legislation, arguing imported drugs could not be guaranteed safe and that it would undermine the US pricing system that funds drug development.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was led by a Republican senator with a Democratic co-lead and drew 9 cosponsors split 5 D, 2 R, and 2 I, so support crossed party lines; no floor vote ever tested it.

industries.note: Personal importation would let patients buy identical drugs at Canadian prices, cutting into the higher US prices drug makers charge the same customers. The industry's interest in keeping importation barred runs directly against Americans paying those prices.

Certification would create a legal, FDA-listed channel for Canadian pharmacies to sell 90-day supplies to American patients, with the pharmacy's interest running alongside patients seeking lower prices.

Patients filling prescriptions from certified Canadian pharmacies would bypass US pharmacies, which sell the same drugs at US prices. Their interest in preserving that arrangement runs against consumers' interest in cheaper prices.
